constellation_visibility.name: Anubaldir's Labyrinth
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Winter evenings; rises E/ENE in autumn, high south by mid-winter, west by spring dusk.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Summer evenings; high north from much of temperate south, lower north from far south.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Visible from most Belavadös latitudes; very high far northern summer daylight can hide it seasonally; below horizon only very far south near 75°S.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: East in Oct-Nov evenings; meridian/south around Jan evenings; west in Mar-Apr evenings.

constellation_visibility.name: Bastveig's Tidehook
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Winter evenings; best Dec-Feb; rises east in late autumn, crosses south around winter, sets west in spring.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Summer evenings; very prominent, often high in northern sky from southern mid-latitudes.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Almost worldwide: belt declinations near 0° make it visible from nearly all populated latitudes.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: East/SE at early winter dusk, due south/north around mid-evening, west/SW late night or late season.

constellation_visibility.name: Setrimir's Diadem
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Year-round in northern latitudes; highest/clearest depending on local season and latitude. Setrimir Diadem stays near true north.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Mostly not visible from southern skies except right on/near the equator where Setrimir Diadem grazes the north horizon.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Circumpolar for observers north of about 1°N for Setrimir Diadem itself; full Little Dipper circumpolar from mid-northern latitudes. Not useful south of the equator.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: No normal east-to-west rise/set in mid-north: it rotates counterclockwise around the north celestial pole.

constellation_visibility.name: Thoryn-Rahek's Web
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Year-round from mid/high northern latitudes; highest on spring evenings; low north in autumn evenings.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Visible only from tropics and some southern subtropics; largely absent from temperate southern skies.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Circumpolar north of roughly 41°N for the full asterism; poor/absent south of roughly 25-35°S depending horizon.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: In the north: NE/east side of pole in winter evenings, overhead/high in spring, NW/west side in summer, low north in fall.

constellation_visibility.name: Enkirael's Warfire
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Winter evenings and early spring; high overhead at mid-northern latitudes.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Visible from tropics and northern parts of southern skies; low north and incomplete in far south.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Best north of the equator; visible down to roughly 30-40°S depending the star, but low.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: Rises NE in autumn evenings, culminates high north/south in winter, sinks NW in spring.

constellation_visibility.name: Nephthysra's Mirror
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Spring to early summer evenings; rises east in spring, crowns high south by early summer.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Autumn/winter southern evenings; visible low to moderate in the north sky depending latitude.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Visible from most northern and tropical latitudes; increasingly low south of 45°S.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: East/NE in spring evenings; south/north meridian around late spring; west/NW by late summer.

constellation_visibility.name: Sokhivar's Lantern
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Year-round in mid/high northern latitudes; most prominent autumn and winter evenings.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Visible only low from tropics/southern subtropics; mostly absent from temperate far south.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Circumpolar from many northern sites; poor or invisible south of roughly 25-35°S.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: Rotates around the north celestial pole opposite the the web field; appears as W or M depending season/time.

constellation_visibility.name: Ishtanora's Hearthdrum
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Late autumn through winter evenings; low east in fall, high south by winter, west in early spring.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Spring/summer southern evenings; prominent north of zenith for many southern observers.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Visible from most latitudes except extreme far southern; best away from city light.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: East in Oct-Nov evenings; meridian around Dec-Jan; west by Mar evenings.

constellation_visibility.name: Freyseth's Mask
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Late spring through summer evenings; low in the southern sky from mid-northern latitudes.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Autumn/winter evenings; high and spectacular from southern latitudes.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Best in tropics and southern skies; tail invisible from high northern latitudes above roughly 55-60°N.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: Rises SE, culminates low south from northern lands or high north/overhead from southern lands, sets SW.

constellation_visibility.name: The Star-River
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Visible all year in segments. Winter Star-River runs through the cold-season river fields; summer Star-River through northern and southern river gates is brightest.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Visible all year in segments; the Stormblood Tail is highest in southern winter.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: All latitudes see some Star-River, but the Stormblood Tail is best from tropics and southern skies.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: Segments rise and set like a tilted river; bright Star-River heart rises SE, culminates south/north, sets SW.

constellation_visibility.name: The Three Watches
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Nephthysra Glass: spring; Setrimir Diadem: year-round north; Valkhamesh Prime: summer/autumn.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Nephthysra Glass and Valkhamesh Prime visible from much of southern skies but lower north; Setrimir Diadem mostly absent.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Setrimir Diadem is northern-only; Nephthysra Glass visible to about 70°S; Valkhamesh Prime visible to about 51°S.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: Nephthysra Glass rises east in spring; Valkhamesh Prime rises NE in late spring/summer; Setrimir Diadem fixed near north.

constellation_visibility.name: The Spirit Lights
constellation_visibility.northern_skies: Most likely in dark months and around geomagnetic storms; equinox periods often productive.
constellation_visibility.southern_skies: Southern polar lights have their own mirror-form; the northern lights belong to northern magnetic skies.
constellation_visibility.latitude_behavior: Best beneath the northern magnetic oval and far-northern provinces; during great sky storms can reach mid-latitude lands.
constellation_visibility.east_west_behavior: Appears northward from mid-latitude lands; overhead beneath the magnetic oval; no fixed rise/set like stars.

nebula_fields.caption: Âhufej — Minotaur Labyrinth of Anubaldir
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Foreground soot lanes (900 ly), dense emission nursery (1,380 ly), red-brown rear cloud (5,800 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: Dense newborn stellar nursery with glowing hydrogen chambers. Rose tones arise from ionized hydrogen, gold from embedded young stars illuminating dust grains, while smoke-violet regions form where cooler molecular gas mingles with shadowed dust curtains. Texture resembles folded velvet mixed with branching smoke channels. Numerous protostars, Bok globules, and accretion knots are embedded throughout.

nebula_fields.caption: Dus‘idu — Silkborn Web of Thoryn-Rahek
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Silver strand foreground (1,100 ly), supernova shell (2,100 ly), violet mutation veil (6,200 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: Extremely filamentary remnant structure. Cyan and jade hues indicate oxygen-rich shock fronts while white regions mark compressed gas where multiple shock waves intersect. Texture appears as torn silk, braided tendrils, and lace-like membranes. Contains expanding ejecta sheets, ionized oxygen filaments, sulfur traces, and high-energy particle fronts.

nebula_fields.caption: Ềdizfu — Dragonborn Dominion of Valkhamesh
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Foreground sparks (1,800 ly), storm sheet (4,200 ly), primary rift flower (5,600 ly), violet dust rear layer (7,900 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: Vast petal-shaped dark nebula carved through a glowing emission field. Crimson and magenta petals surround blue-black voids where dense molecular dust blocks starlight. Texture resembles layered flower petals made of smoke and velvet. Contains cold molecular clouds, active collapse zones, dark filaments, and bright ionization ridges outlining the rift edges.

nebula_fields.caption: Juçdimx — Crossroads Mask of Freyseth
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Front ash layer (2,000 ly), reflective dust basin (3,400 ly), curse smoke (5,100 ly), under-road shadow (10,300 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: A highly reflective dust field illuminated by nearby blue stars. Silver and pearl regions arise from light scattering by fine silicate particles. Texture resembles finished frost, drifting fog banks, and layered mirror-glass sheets. Contains reflective silicate dust, carbonaceous smoke clouds, and fragmented molecular lanes.

nebula_fields.caption: Jadd-Jisud — Wechselkind Crown of Setrimir
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Metal-blue shell (2,200 ly), green shell (4,800 ly), primary red-amber shell cluster (8,900 ly), lost-key echo layer (9,600 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: Collection of overlapping planetary-nebula remnants. Amber and red shells arise from hydrogen and nitrogen emissions, while charcoal gaps reveal exhausted central cavities. Texture appears as stacked bubbles, fractured onion skins, and cracked glass spheres. Components include dying stellar cores, expanding gas shells, metallic ion clouds, and dusty ejecta rings.

nebula_fields.caption: Horundar — Sahuagin Deep Gate of Bastveig
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Tide mist (1,600 ly), reservoir core (1,900 ly), reef sheet (3,900 ly), blackwater wall (8,700 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: Diffuse cloud filled with icy cometary material. White and ice-blue coloration results from starlight reflecting from frozen dust and microscopic ice crystals. Texture resembles sea fog, frost plumes, and subcombined currents. Rich in volatile compounds, comet embryos, crystalline ice grains, and reflective dust sheets.

nebula_fields.caption: Wougen — Luma Mirror of Nephthysra
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Blue foreground haze (1,200 ly), star-forming core (2,850 ly), mirror sheet (3,600 ly), rose backwash (6,300 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: Massive molecular cloud actively producing stellar clusters. Green-gold regions arise from mixed oxygen and dust reflection, cream tones from warm embedded stars. Texture resembles billowing cream-colored thunderheads crossed by turquoise rivers. Components include molecular hydrogen reservoirs, stellar nurseries, evaporating gas pillars, and young cluster cavities.

nebula_fields.caption: Ŝiowoei — Dragonborn Dominion outer spiral
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Silver foreground threads (2,000 ly), central spiral coil (4,200 ly), violet rear dust (7,900 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_components: A rotating spiral dust formation resembling a galactic whirlpool. Dark blue channels mark denser dust lanes while silver highlights indicate reflected starlight. Texture resembles braided ribbons, hurricane bands, and coiled smoke. Contains spiral molecular filaments, reflective silicates, and embedded star embryos tracing the coil arms.

Celestial reference for sky time, moons, wandering worlds, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-lights, and constellations

1. Guide and sky-time rules
Naming and replacement rules used in this document
• The bright band crossing the sky is called the Star-River of Belavadös.
• The observing landscape is described as the Great River Valley and its desert-edge skyfields.
• The twelve wandering planets and two moons use the supplied invented names and coordinates.
• The sky analysis keeps historical-style latitude, precession, seasonality, and horizon logic, but is written as Belavadös sky lore rather than a modern archaeological report.
Coordinate system used

The sky is described with right ascension and declination. These coordinates function like celestial longitude and latitude. Apparent magnitude uses lower numbers for brighter objects, with negative values being especially bright. Planet and moon distances use AU or kilometers; stellar distances use light-years.
Earth and Belavadös sky time

Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, session schedules, travel timing, event boards, and deadlines. Use Belavadös dates second for lore records, temple calendars, journals, festivals, and immersion. A Belavadös astronomical year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long, and those solar days are distributed evenly across the Earth year for table play.

For sky calculations, use solar progress rather than the named civil date. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates arranged as eleven 30-date months, while the 0.15 solar-day correction is spread through the year as a tiny clock drift. There is no bonus day or frozen end-period for moons, planets, tides, omens, or the Star-River.
Sky conversion formula
1. daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
2. earthProgress = (Earth day-of-year - 1 + fractionOfEarthDay) / daysInEarthYear.
3. belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this value for moon phases, planetary positions, tides, constellations, seasons, and sky omens.
4. belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this value only for the named Belavadös month and date.
5. Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
Player-facing observing log format
Write sky events Earth-first, then Belavadös-second: Earth Month Day, Year, local time with UTC label / Belavadös month date, weekday, Belavadös clock, solar-day progress, moon phase, and sky note.

Settlement and province sky notes may include the settlement UTC when the observing site differs from the province primary UTC. Province summaries should show only one or two Earth-style UTC labels, while exact settlement exports can store the UTC chosen by longitude.
Belavadös month cycle for sky records

These month names are used for date labels only. A moon, wandering world, tide, season, or sky omen should still be calculated from belSolarDayProgress so the sky remains smooth across the full Earth year.
2. Sky setting and Star-River
Historical-style sky setting
The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise.

The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and future named sky patterns can serve as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.
The Star-River of Belavadös

The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions.

From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.

3. Celestial inventory
This inventory separates fixed stars, upper-atmosphere light, moons, worlds, regions, nebula fields, and the blank constellation placeholder so each part of the sky reference has one clear home.
4. Constellations

These are the sky-names used when the Gods still walked openly across Belavadös, before their prisons, before public ichor engines, before rail bells, portal halls, and industrial skyports taught cities to trust machines more than stars. The names are the names carved into tide stairs, burial ledgers, cairn roads, hearth beams, watchtower lintels, reef shrines, and desert-edge observatories.
Each figure keeps its fixed place in the sky. The names belong to Belavadös. The coordinates preserve the star-path for sky maps, generators, omen records, and night watches.
4.1. How skykeepers read the fixed heavens

Belavadös skykeepers use right ascension and declination as the fixed grid of the upper world. Right ascension runs from 0h to 24h around the sky. Declination rises north or south of the sky-equator. Magnitude records visible brightness; the smaller the number, the stronger the light.

Seasonal movement follows the 330.15 day Belavadös solar year. Civil dates still belong to the eleven named months, but the sky obeys solar progress. Moon phases, tides, wandering worlds, Star-River omens, and constellation seasons move smoothly across the whole year.

The old horizon rule is simple enough for any watchtower: at about 30 degrees north, lights above about +60 degrees stay near the northern sky and lights below about -60 degrees never rise. Other latitudes shift the height of the figures without moving the figures themselves.

4.5. Skykeeper practice

Harbors, caravan wells, funeral roads, terrace farms, reef shrines, and high watchtowers all keep different portions of the same sky. Coastal settlements read Bastveig's Tidehook, Freyseth's Mask, the Star-River, and the two moons for water law. Mountain and inland roads favor Anubaldir's Labyrinth, Enkirael's Warfire, and Setrimir's Diadem. Hearth villages mark Ishtanora's Hearthdrum, while temple singers and roof watchers keep Sokhivar's Lantern.

The old rule remains unchanged: a constellation is a witness. A vow spoken beneath a named figure is never only private. The sky is a ledger, a road, a tide stair, a battlefield, a mirror, a hearth, and a warning. When the Gods were free, this was not metaphor. It was daily survival.
5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky

The lunar system is nested: the larger moon orbits the world, while the smaller moonlet orbits the larger moon and is carried along with it. This creates paired lunar calendars, small bead-like crossings, and a subtle secondary tidal pulse. For Earth sessions, both lunar positions are calculated from belSolarDayProgress, not from the civil month and date.
Lunar phase pacing for Earth sessions
Chandratecu-Seleneš phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 19.20) / 19.20.
Mictlindra-Nannara phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 2.02) / 2.02.
Use the resulting fraction as the phase position in the lunar cycle. This keeps both moons moving continuously across non-leap and leap Earth years.

6. Worlds, regions, and comet

The worlds orbit their star upon a relatively flat shared plane known as the Celestial Road. Belavadös itself remains the 1.00 AU reference world with a 330.15 Belavadös-day astronomical year; player-facing dates distribute that year evenly across the Earth calendar.

Eiršu'neth Comet

The Eiršu'neth Comet is a massive, long-period Vishtecu–Hyperu family comet distinguished by its unusually large icy nucleus, high mass, and stable yet dramatic inclined orbit through the outer Belavadös system. With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. Its 18° inclination above the Celestial Road and carefully positioned crossing points make it a safe, non-impacting body despite its size, periodically producing a spectacular multi-month display as it passes through the inner reaches of its orbit.

8. Representative night

A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the northern cold-season field and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N.

When the bright inner planet Mardukesh-Huitra is favorably placed, it dominates the evening or dawn sky with pearl-white brilliance. Surixoch-Aresu appears copper-red and lower near twilight. The four ringed planets are not equally easy to interpret with the unaided eye, but under magnification their ring lore becomes central: Vishtecu-Hyperu shows a rose-gold hairline, Enlimitra a frosted silver span, Quetzal-Hermeshu a tilted green-bronze eye, and Varunatl-Kronu a white-ringed blue elongation.
9. Source and method notes

The astronomical logic in this document uses standard sky-coordinate concepts: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, axial precession, and a 330.15 day Belavadös astronomical year distributed evenly across the Earth year for play. The values are intended for generators, lore notes, sky omens, transit boards, and table-facing observing logs.

No Earth star names are included. The document is intended as a lore-compatible sky reference for Belavadös and as a practical coordinate table for generators; the fixed stars are deliberately placed at remote background distances and several are faint enough to be only partially visible without unusually dark skies or magnification.

• Belavadös sky-time framework: 330.15 day astronomical year, 330-date civil calendar, eleven named months, and Earth-first table play conversion.
• Belavadös celestial register: moons, wandering worlds, comet, celestial regions, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-light labels, and constellation coordinates.
• Sky-coordinate method: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, and seasonal star movement.
• Lore basis: Age of Open Gods skykeeping, imprisoned-god pantheon memory, pre-industrial temple astronomy, tide law, road law, burial ledgers, and post-ichor infrastructure context.

tables.caption_or_previous_text: The Eiršu'neth Comet is a massive, long-period Vishtecu–Hyperu family comet distinguished by its unusually large icy nucleus, high mass, and stable yet dramatic inclined orbit through the outer Belavadös system. With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. Its 18° inclination above the Celestial Road and carefully positioned crossing points make it a safe, non-impacting body despite its size, periodically producing a spectacular multi-month display as it passes through the inner reaches of its orbit.

sections.heading: Belavadös Night Sky
content: Celestial reference for sky time, moons, wandering worlds, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-lights, and constellations

sections.heading: 5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky
7. Distant stars and sky-lights of Belavadös
Naming and replacement rules used in this document
content: • The bright band crossing the sky is called the Star-River of Belavadös.
• The observing landscape is described as the Great River Valley and its desert-edge skyfields.
• The twelve wandering planets and two moons use the supplied invented names and coordinates.
• The sky analysis keeps historical-style latitude, precession, seasonality, and horizon logic, but is written as Belavadös sky lore rather than a modern archaeological report.

sections.heading: Coordinate system used
content: The sky is described with right ascension and declination. These coordinates function like celestial longitude and latitude. Apparent magnitude uses lower numbers for brighter objects, with negative values being especially bright. Planet and moon distances use AU or kilometers; stellar distances use light-years.

sections.heading: Earth and Belavadös sky time
content: Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, session schedules, travel timing, event boards, and deadlines. Use Belavadös dates second for lore records, temple calendars, journals, festivals, and immersion. A Belavadös astronomical year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long, and those solar days are distributed evenly across the Earth year for table play.

For sky calculations, use solar progress rather than the named civil date. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates arranged as eleven 30-date months, while the 0.15 solar-day correction is spread through the year as a tiny clock drift. There is no bonus day or frozen end-period for moons, planets, tides, omens, or the Star-River.

sections.heading: 1. daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
3. belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this value for moon phases, planetary positions, tides, constellations, seasons, and sky omens.
4. belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this value only for the named Belavadös month and date.
5. Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
Player-facing observing log format
content: Write sky events Earth-first, then Belavadös-second: Earth Month Day, Year, local time with UTC label / Belavadös month date, weekday, Belavadös clock, solar-day progress, moon phase, and sky note.

Settlement and province sky notes may include the settlement UTC when the observing site differs from the province primary UTC. Province summaries should show only one or two Earth-style UTC labels, while exact settlement exports can store the UTC chosen by longitude.

sections.heading: Belavadös month cycle for sky records
content: These month names are used for date labels only. A moon, wandering world, tide, season, or sky omen should still be calculated from belSolarDayProgress so the sky remains smooth across the full Earth year.

sections.heading: Historical-style sky setting
content: The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise.

The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and future named sky patterns can serve as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.

sections.heading: The Star-River of Belavadös
content: The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions.

From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.

sections.heading: Nebula fields of Belavadös
content: Each nebula uses the same field layout for generator use: coordinate anchor, distance/span, type, dominant colors, layer structure, and texture/components.

3. Celestial inventory
content: This inventory separates fixed stars, upper-atmosphere light, moons, worlds, regions, nebula fields, and the blank constellation placeholder so each part of the sky reference has one clear home.

sections.heading: 4. Constellations
content: These are the sky-names used when the Gods still walked openly across Belavadös, before their prisons, before public ichor engines, before rail bells, portal halls, and industrial skyports taught cities to trust machines more than stars. The names are the names carved into tide stairs, burial ledgers, cairn roads, hearth beams, watchtower lintels, reef shrines, and desert-edge observatories.
Each figure keeps its fixed place in the sky. The names belong to Belavadös. The coordinates preserve the star-path for sky maps, generators, omen records, and night watches.

sections.heading: 4.1. How skykeepers read the fixed heavens
content: Belavadös skykeepers use right ascension and declination as the fixed grid of the upper world. Right ascension runs from 0h to 24h around the sky. Declination rises north or south of the sky-equator. Magnitude records visible brightness; the smaller the number, the stronger the light.

Seasonal movement follows the 330.15 day Belavadös solar year. Civil dates still belong to the eleven named months, but the sky obeys solar progress. Moon phases, tides, wandering worlds, Star-River omens, and constellation seasons move smoothly across the whole year.

The old horizon rule is simple enough for any watchtower: at about 30 degrees north, lights above about +60 degrees stay near the northern sky and lights below about -60 degrees never rise. Other latitudes shift the height of the figures without moving the figures themselves.

sections.heading: 4.3. Seasonal and hemispheric visibility
content: Northern and southern visibility depends on latitude and season. East-west behavior describes how the pattern rises, crosses the meridian, sets, or circles the northern sky during the night.

sections.heading: 4.4. Star layouts and coordinate anchors
content: The following tables preserve the fixed coordinates of each light and sky waypoint. Names are Belavadös names. RA and Dec are the placement anchors used by sky maps, temple charts, observatories, and generators.

sections.heading: 4.5. Skykeeper practice
content: Harbors, caravan wells, funeral roads, terrace farms, reef shrines, and high watchtowers all keep different portions of the same sky. Coastal settlements read Bastveig's Tidehook, Freyseth's Mask, the Star-River, and the two moons for water law. Mountain and inland roads favor Anubaldir's Labyrinth, Enkirael's Warfire, and Setrimir's Diadem. Hearth villages mark Ishtanora's Hearthdrum, while temple singers and roof watchers keep Sokhivar's Lantern.

The old rule remains unchanged: a constellation is a witness. A vow spoken beneath a named figure is never only private. The sky is a ledger, a road, a tide stair, a battlefield, a mirror, a hearth, and a warning. When the Gods were free, this was not metaphor. It was daily survival.

sections.heading: 5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky
content: The lunar system is nested: the larger moon orbits the world, while the smaller moonlet orbits the larger moon and is carried along with it. This creates paired lunar calendars, small bead-like crossings, and a subtle secondary tidal pulse. For Earth sessions, both lunar positions are calculated from belSolarDayProgress, not from the civil month and date.

sections.heading: Lunar phase pacing for Earth sessions
content: Chandratecu-Seleneš phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 19.20) / 19.20.
Mictlindra-Nannara phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 2.02) / 2.02.
Use the resulting fraction as the phase position in the lunar cycle. This keeps both moons moving continuously across non-leap and leap Earth years.

sections.heading: 6. Worlds, regions, and comet
content: The worlds orbit their star upon a relatively flat shared plane known as the Celestial Road. Belavadös itself remains the 1.00 AU reference world with a 330.15 Belavadös-day astronomical year; player-facing dates distribute that year evenly across the Earth calendar.

sections.heading: Minor worlds
content: Minor worlds are rounded celestial bodies that share their orbital regions with numerous smaller bodies.

sections.heading: Eiršu'neth Comet
content: The Eiršu'neth Comet is a massive, long-period Vishtecu–Hyperu family comet distinguished by its unusually large icy nucleus, high mass, and stable yet dramatic inclined orbit through the outer Belavadös system. With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. Its 18° inclination above the Celestial Road and carefully positioned crossing points make it a safe, non-impacting body despite its size, periodically producing a spectacular multi-month display as it passes through the inner reaches of its orbit.

sections.heading: 8. Representative night
content: A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the northern cold-season field and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N.

When the bright inner planet Mardukesh-Huitra is favorably placed, it dominates the evening or dawn sky with pearl-white brilliance. Surixoch-Aresu appears copper-red and lower near twilight. The four ringed planets are not equally easy to interpret with the unaided eye, but under magnification their ring lore becomes central: Vishtecu-Hyperu shows a rose-gold hairline, Enlimitra a frosted silver span, Quetzal-Hermeshu a tilted green-bronze eye, and Varunatl-Kronu a white-ringed blue elongation.

sections.heading: 9. Source and method notes
content: The astronomical logic in this document uses standard sky-coordinate concepts: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, axial precession, and a 330.15 day Belavadös astronomical year distributed evenly across the Earth year for play. The values are intended for generators, lore notes, sky omens, transit boards, and table-facing observing logs.

No Earth star names are included. The document is intended as a lore-compatible sky reference for Belavadös and as a practical coordinate table for generators; the fixed stars are deliberately placed at remote background distances and several are faint enough to be only partially visible without unusually dark skies or magnification.

content: • Belavadös sky-time framework: 330.15 day astronomical year, 330-date civil calendar, eleven named months, and Earth-first table play conversion.
• Belavadös celestial register: moons, wandering worlds, comet, celestial regions, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-light labels, and constellation coordinates.
• Sky-coordinate method: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, and seasonal star movement.
• Lore basis: Age of Open Gods skykeeping, imprisoned-god pantheon memory, pre-industrial temple astronomy, tide law, road law, burial ledgers, and post-ichor infrastructure context.

paragraphs: Belavadös Time Conversion Guide
Earth-first table play, Belavadös-second lore time
1. The New Rule
Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, schedules, sessions, travel, and deadlines.
Use Belavadös dates second for lore, temples, festivals, legal records, journals, and immersion.
A Belavadös year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long. For table play, those 330.15 days are distributed evenly across the Earth year.
2. Clean Math
3. Conversion Formula
daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
earthProgress = (Earth day-of-year - 1 + fractionOfEarthDay) / daysInEarthYear.
belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this for sky, moon, season, and astronomy math.
belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this for the named calendar date.
monthIndex = floor(belCivilDateProgress / 30), from 0 to 10.
dayOfMonth = floor(belCivilDateProgress % 30) + 1.
Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
4. Month Cycle
5. Weekdays
For player-facing schedules, keep the live Earth weekday mapping. This keeps sessions, transit boards, deadlines, and reminders easy to read.
6. Night Sky Integration
Use 330.15 Belavadös days as the astronomical year because the Night Sky file identifies Belavadös at 1.00 AU with a 330.15-day orbital period.
Use 330 named civil dates for the calendar because the civil calendar is still 11 months of 30 days.
Use solar progress, not month/date progress, for moon phases, planetary positions, constellations, tides, and sky omens.

The larger moon Chandratecu-Seleneš has a 19.20 Belavadös-day orbit; the smaller moonlet Mictlindra-Nannara has a 2.02 Belavadös-day orbit. For Earth sessions, calculate their phase from belSolarDayProgress so the sky stays smooth all year.
Because the solar correction is distributed, the Star-River, wandering worlds, and paired moons never need a special frozen/end-buffer period.
7. Province Time Zones

Each province now receives a primary Earth-style UTC label and, where useful, one neighboring secondary label. Settlement-specific exports should store the exact settlement UTC by longitude. Province summaries should show only the one or two labels below.
Province UTC Table
8. Formatting Standards
General date: Earth Month Day, Year / Belavadös Month Day, Weekday.
Exact time: Earth time with UTC or local label / Belavadös clock time.
Settlement time: include the settlement UTC if it differs from the province primary UTC.
Province summary: show one or two UTC labels only, never a long chain of every border band.
Sky event: calculate from belSolarDayProgress and display Earth-first for players.
